title: Imagining It Already Happened
text:
In 1989 Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo and Nancy Pennington published a study on a small change in how people think about future events. They called it prospective hindsight: imagining that an event has already happened, then explaining why.

Participants read descriptions of possible future events and were asked to generate reasons why each might occur. For some, the event was presented as uncertain, something that might happen. For others, it was presented as if it had already occurred, with certainty, and they were asked to explain why it had happened. The situations were held otherwise constant.

People who imagined that the event had already happened produced more reasons, and their reasons tended to be more specific and more focused on particular causes, than those who considered the event merely possible. Treating the outcome as a fact seemed to free them to search their knowledge for explanations, rather than debating whether it would happen at all.

The psychologist Gary Klein later drew on this research to design a planning technique he called the premortem, described in a 2007 Harvard Business Review article. Before a project begins, the team imagines that it is a year later and the project has failed badly. Each member then writes down every reason they can think of for the failure. The exercise makes it easier, and socially safer, for people to voice doubts that would otherwise go unspoken, while there is still time to address them.
lesson: Before committing to a plan, imagine it has already failed and list every reason why. Treating failure as a fact makes risks easier to see and to discuss openly while you can still act.
people: Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo, Nancy Pennington
source: Mitchell, D. J., Russo, J. E., and Pennington, N. (1989). Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 2(1), 25-38.
